output.title: Firmware 1.4.2 BLE disconnect-rate rise vs 1.4.1, app-version confound ruled out
output.summary: The falsifying test for the leading hypothesis (that the disconnect-count rise on 1.4.2 is largely a detection-sensitivity artifact) is: if session_gap_minutes, overall or in any regional/activity segment, rose in proportion to the disconnect-count ratio, the artifact account would be falsified because it would show a real increase in experienced connectivity loss matching the counted-event rise. Region-level breakdowns obtained for both firmware versions show no such proportional rise in any region, which is consistent with (though does not conclusively prove) the leading hypothesis, but sample sizes per region are small and no phone-OS control was available, so status remains UNCERTAIN.

leading_hypothesis.statement: The revised BLE connection-supervisor timing shipped in firmware 1.4.2 is associated with a large rise in counted ble_disconnects_24h events relative to 1.4.1 on the same app version, while measured session_gap_minutes is not significantly different, suggesting the counted-event rise reflects faster/more sensitive drop detection at least in part rather than a proportional increase in real connectivity loss experienced by users.

alternative_hypotheses.statement: The counted ble_disconnects_24h rise on firmware 1.4.2 reflects a phone-side Bluetooth stack change (as previously seen in a structurally similar closed incident) rather than the firmware supervisor-timing revision itself.
alternative_hypotheses.falsifying_test: Hold phone-OS/model constant across 1.4.1 and 1.4.2 devices and re-run the ble_disconnects_24h comparison; if the rate-ratio confidence interval still excludes one after controlling for phone OS/model, the phone-stack alternative is falsified for this population.

alternative_hypotheses.statement: Real connectivity degradation from the 1.4.2 timing change is concentrated in outdoor/body-blocked/commuting RF conditions (untested in soak-lab) and is masked in the aggregate session_gap_minutes comparison by regions/activity levels with mostly indoor usage.
alternative_hypotheses.falsifying_test: If a region or activity-level segment plausibly dominated by outdoor/commuting RF conditions shows a session_gap_minutes ratio between firmware 1.4.2 and 1.4.1 rising in proportion to the disconnect-count ratio, this hypothesis is supported; the regional breakdown obtained shows no region with a disproportionate rise, which weakens rather than falsifies but does not confirm the concentrated-degradation account given limited per-region sample sizes.

output.title: Skin-irritation / adhesion feedback tag review — no evidence of new escalation beyond known open characterization
output.summary: The leading hypothesis rests on a joint mechanism: lift/irritation rising with both high motion intensity and elevated skin-temp delta. An activity_level breakdown shows adhesion_flag rates concentrating sharply at the highest motion-intensity tier, consistent with that arm, but skin_temp_delta_c rates are essentially flat across all activity tiers, not supporting the thermal arm of the stated mechanism. This partial decoupling is a candidate falsifying observation for the specific joint-mechanism claim and keeps open an alternative explanation (e.g., a mechanical/lot-based adhesive defect surfacing under high motion independent of skin temperature) that the current tooling cannot rule out at the lot level. Status remains UNCERTAIN pending lot-level data or a cleaner test isolating motion-only vs. thermal-only irritation drivers.

leading_hypothesis.statement: Skin-irritation feedback is a continuation of the pre-existing, open adhesive-lift characterization (elevated lift under high motion intensity and skin-temp delta) rather than a new emergent defect, based on flat adhesion telemetry and tickets that consistently co-occur with adhesion/comfort-fit language describing high-intensity or sweaty sessions.

alternative_hypotheses.statement: A new, lot-specific adhesive defect (independent of the pre-existing high-motion/high-skin-temp-delta characterization) is driving the skin-irritation feedback rise; irritation could be concentrated in a specific hardware lot rather than scaling with motion intensity or skin-temp delta.
alternative_hypotheses.falsifying_test: Falsifying test for the leading hypothesis: pull the activity_level breakdown for skin_temp_delta_c and adhesion_flag in the current window. The leading hypothesis requires that elevated adhesion/irritation co-occurs with elevated skin_temp_delta_c at high motion intensity (the stated joint mechanism). If skin_temp_delta_c does not rise with activity_level while adhesion_flag does rise sharply at the highest activity tier, the 'elevated skin-temp delta' arm of the mechanism is not supported by the data even though the 'high motion intensity' arm is, which undercuts the specific joint-mechanism claim in the leading hypothesis and is consistent with an alternative driver (e.g., mechanical/lot-based adhesive failure) rather than a purely thermal-and-motion characterization.

Feedback records matching skin-irritation tag, prior window
adhesion_flag rate ratio, firmware 1.4.1 vs 1.4.2, current window

supporting_evidence.claim: Sampled skin-irritation feedback tickets consistently co-occur with adhesion and comfort-fit tags and describe adhesive lift during high-intensity or sweaty sessions, matching the documented mechanism of lift rising with motion intensity and skin-temp delta.

The known-issues register documents an open (not closed) adhesive-lift characterization tied to high motion and elevated skin-temp delta, and explicitly warns against treating a new ticket cluster as automatically covered by that open item.
The support playbook instructs that adhesion-under-motion tickets must not be closed as expected and that a new cluster still needs a lot split rather than a wave-away via the existing known issue.

counter_evidence.claim: Adhesion_flag telemetry rate did not rise meaningfully between prior and current windows and shows no regional concentration (rates ranged narrowly across all five regions in both windows).
skin_temp_delta_c telemetry rate slightly decreased rather than increased between prior and current windows, which does not support an intensifying mechanism.
The firmware 1.4.1 vs 1.4.2 adhesion_flag rate-ratio confidence interval includes one, so no firmware version is statistically distinguishable as a driver.

skin_temp_delta_c rate was essentially uniform across activity_level tiers in the current window (low, moderate, high, and very_high tiers all showed comparable rates), which does not support the stated mechanism that skin-temp delta rises together with motion intensity to drive lift, even though adhesion_flag itself was markedly higher at the very_high activity tier.

recommended_actions.description: Continue routine monitoring of adhesion_flag rate and skin-irritation feedback tag volume week over week; re-open severity review if a firmware, region, or lot-specific concentration emerges.

Request lot/serial-level metadata for skin-irritation and adhesion tickets to test for concentration in a single production lot, per playbook guidance that a new cluster needs a lot split rather than a wave-away via the existing open characterization.
Remind support agents via the existing playbook not to close skin-irritation/adhesion tickets as expected behavior; continue offering replacement rings and logging tags as appropriate.

uncertainty: No lot/serial-level telemetry or feedback field is available through current tooling, so a new adhesive-lot defect (as previously confirmed in INC-2025-031) cannot be ruled out despite flat aggregate rates.
Feedback sample sizes per window are small relative to the total matched records, limiting confidence that the sampled text is representative of the full ticket population.

The candidate's stated affected-user and prior-event counts do not exactly match the tool-observed feedback record counts for the skin-irritation tag across the prior and current windows; the discrepancy was not reconciled and may reflect different counting units (users vs. events vs. records).

The activity_level breakdown shows adhesion_flag concentrating at the highest motion-intensity tier, which is consistent with the leading hypothesis's motion-intensity arm, but skin_temp_delta_c does not track activity_level in the same way, so the joint 'motion + thermal' mechanism as stated is only partially supported.

No lot/serial-level telemetry or feedback field is available through current tooling, so a new adhesive-lot defect concentrated at very-high activity (independent of skin-temp delta) cannot be ruled out.
Feedback sample sizes per window remain small relative to total matched records, limiting confidence that sampled ticket text is representative.

output.title: Rising claims-interpretation ticket cluster — wellness score misread as clinical result
output.summary: A falsifying test for the leading comms/copy-misread hypothesis is to check whether an actual sensor telemetry anomaly, not just ticket text, is coincident with and concentrated in the firmware or app versions driving the claims-interpretation and data-accuracy ticket surge; if such a version-linked anomaly were found, it would falsify the claim that this is purely a communications issue. A check of skin_temp_delta_c across firmware versions and windows found no such spike or version concentration, which weakens but does not fully rule out a genuine sensor-regression alternative and is consistent with the leading hypothesis, though other metrics remain unchecked.

leading_hypothesis.statement: The rising claims-interpretation cluster reflects on-screen copy/wording (the readiness score presented near confusable language) causing wearers to interpret a wellness indication as a clinical/diagnostic result, a known communications risk pattern documented in KD-03 and KD-05 and previously confirmed as a comms incident (INC-2025-002) rather than a hardware or firmware defect.

alternative_hypotheses.statement: The claims-interpretation/data-accuracy ticket surge reflects a genuine sensor or scoring-input regression (not just wording confusion), such that wearers are reacting to output that is actually anomalous rather than misreading a stable wellness score.
alternative_hypotheses.falsifying_test: Compare skin_temp_delta_c telemetry across firmware versions between the prior and current windows; if the rate is flat and shows no version-linked spike coincident with the ticket rise, then a real sensor/data-output regression cannot explain the surge, which is inconsistent with this alternative hypothesis. Observed telemetry was essentially flat across all firmware versions in both windows, with no version showing a distinctive jump.

supporting_evidence.claim: Sampled current-window tickets describe wearers treating the readiness score as a clinical/diagnostic result (cancelling a meeting, showing it as a clinical finding, needing clarification it is not a diagnosis).

KD-03 defines exactly this symptom set (treating the number as a clinical result, asking what disease it is, cancelling plans, forwarding screenshots) as the claims-misread queue tagged claims-interpretation and often data-accuracy.

KD-05 policy states the company must not describe the score as a diagnosis, test, or treatment prompt, and that a claims-shaped ticket cluster can be a real communications/regulatory risk without being a sensor defect.

A near-identical prior cluster (INC-2025-002) was closed as a confirmed communications incident, not a device incident, resolved via copy review and a policy revision, with scoring code left unchanged.

counter_evidence.claim: Some current-window tickets are neutral/resolved confirmations (e.g. a wearer confirming the score is wellness-only after reading the help article), indicating not all matched tickets represent an active misread in progress.

The sample spans multiple firmware versions and multiple app versions with no single version standing out, weakening any device/version-specific defect explanation but also meaning no single fixable release target has been identified yet.

skin_temp_delta_c telemetry shows no firmware-version-linked spike between the prior and current windows, with rates staying in a similar stable range across all firmware versions in both windows, so the ticket surge does not coincide with a detectable sensor-output anomaly on this metric.

Prior-window skin_temp_delta_c rates by firmware were also stable and, if anything, slightly higher than current-window rates, meaning the direction of any telemetry change runs opposite to what a sensor-driven explanation for a rising ticket cluster would require.

recommended_actions.description: Route the ticket cluster to Communications/Regulatory per the support intersection section of KD-05 for a copy review of the on-screen readiness display, since prior on-screen wording has caused misreads (KD-03).
Break down current-window claims-interpretation tickets by firmware_version and app_version to check for concentration around any specific UI copy change before concluding no release is implicated.

If copy review confirms confusing wording, prepare an in-app or help-article clarification (not user-targeted medical messaging) reiterating the score is a wellness indication, consistent with the KD-03 staff script.

uncertainty: The specific trigger for the sharp rise in ticket volume between the prior and current windows has not been identified — only that it mirrors a previously documented and resolved comms pattern.
No firmware/app version breakdown of the full ticket set (only a small sample) was obtained, so a minority-version concentration cannot be fully ruled out.
The co-occurrence with the data-accuracy tag has not been checked against actual sensor telemetry, so a coincident (but separate) accuracy issue cannot be fully excluded.

Only one telemetry metric (skin_temp_delta_c) was checked; other sensor/data-accuracy-relevant metrics such as motion_intensity or adhesion_flag were not examined and could still show a version-linked anomaly.
Absence of a telemetry spike is consistent with, but does not itself prove, the comms/copy explanation for the ticket rise; it only weakens one alternative (a real sensor regression).

output.title: Overheating tag cluster traced to known cosmetic battery-UI mislabeling, not thermal event
output.summary: The falsifying test for the leading hypothesis (that all 'overheating' tickets stem from the cosmetic battery-chrome known issue plus Nordics cold-weather drain, with no real thermal signal) is: find any firmware/device cohort with a materially elevated skin_temp_delta_c rate, or any 'overheating'-tagged ticket lacking co-occurring 'battery'/'app-ui' tags that describes an actually hot device or skin. A firmware breakdown of skin_temp_delta_c for the current window showed no such outlier cohort, and a targeted feedback search for hot-device/skin language under the overheating tag returned zero records, so the test did not falsify the hypothesis in this pass, but the possibility of a masked subgroup remains an open alternative given aggregation and sampling limits.

leading_hypothesis.statement: Tickets tagged 'overheating' reflect the app's low-battery UI rendering as an alarming red/'overheating' style warning, compounded by an accepted regional cold-weather battery-drain characteristic in Nordics, rather than any actual excess device or skin temperature.

alternative_hypotheses.statement: A small genuine hardware thermal cluster exists but is being masked by aggregation: the mean skin_temp_delta_c and flat overall 'overheating' tag volume conceal a firmware- or device-specific subgroup with elevated readings and tickets that do not co-occur with 'battery'/'app-ui' tags.
alternative_hypotheses.falsifying_test: Pull the per-firmware breakdown of skin_temp_delta_c and search 'overheating'-tagged feedback for records lacking co-occurring 'battery' or 'app-ui' tags; if any firmware/version cohort shows a materially elevated rate relative to the others, or if any sampled ticket describes a hot device/skin without a battery-UI or cold-weather-sync explanation, the leading hypothesis is falsified.

supporting_evidence.claim: Skin-temperature delta (a patch-to-skin thermistor measurement, not ambient or core temperature) fell slightly between prior and current windows, showing no elevation coinciding with the overheating tag cluster ({f_1} vs {f_2}).
Every sampled 'overheating' ticket in both windows also carries 'battery' and 'app-ui' tags and describes cold-weather battery drain or a warm phone during sync rather than a hot wearable.

A standing known issue (KI-UI-011) documents that the app's battery chrome renders as an 'overheating'-style warning when the battery percentage is low, accepted as cosmetic UX debt across all regions.
skin_temp_delta_c must not be used as a proxy for ambient or core temperature and the observed rate sits within the documented normal field band.
A closed incident (INC-2024-088) found the same Nordics winter battery-drain pattern to be a regional characteristic, not an incident, and encoded it as a standing known issue.

counter_evidence.claim: Ticket volume for the overheating tag was essentially flat between prior and current windows ({f_4} vs {f_3}), so this is not clearly a resolving trend either — it looks like steady background noise from the known UI/battery issue rather than a genuine thermal cluster in either direction.

Firmware-level breakdown of skin_temp_delta_c for the current window shows no outlier cohort: rates across 1.2.0, 1.3.0, 1.4.0, 1.4.1, and 1.4.2 all cluster tightly (approximately 1.29 to 1.45 celsius_per_device_day), with no firmware showing a distinct elevation that could indicate a hidden thermal subgroup masked by the aggregate mean.

A targeted feedback search for overheating-tagged tickets describing a hot device or skin/burning sensation (rather than battery-UI or cold-sync complaints) returned zero matching records in the current window, finding no evidence of a distinct hardware-thermal ticket subgroup.
